💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week.
  • That’s the major takeaway from newly introduced research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.
  • Sources indicate that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from newly introduced research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

Sources indicate that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

For the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

During the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

The study also highlighted that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers noted.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s notable to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

It’s crucial to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Sources indicate that air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor states.

Air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

According to recent reports, then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil indicates. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”.

Industry observers note that dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil notes. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Dr. Ghafoor indicates she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:.

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:.

Migraine triggers are personal, making it notable to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

Sources indicate that if levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor indicates.

When heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she notes. “All of that is a very important part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”.

Industry observers note that ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor claims. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you're a musician who needs accurate monitoring, a designer who wants something better than AirPods for long editing sessions, or simply someone who loves quality audio, Linsoul IEMs make some of the best IEMs (in-ear-monitors) around.

But, other than the best budget IEMs, they usually don't come cheap, so when Black Friday comes around, it's the perfect time to pick up a bargain.

Industry observers note that in this article, I've picked out the IEMs I think are most worth your money, running from budget single-driver sets to the best multi-driver IEMs under $500. Many are models I've tested myself, and all of them punch well above their price tags.

I just love this IEM. Billed as the world's flattest IEM, the Reference is built for people who want to hear exactly what's on the recording. Twin 10mm dynamic drivers in a horizontally opposed layout handle the bass, while two Sonion balanced armatures take the mids and a Knowles supertweeter covers the top end. It's the top pick in my best IEMs under $500 guide for a good reason.

Industry observers note that this is Xenns Mangird's most premium IEM to date, and it doesn't hold back on hardware: two dynamic drivers and eight balanced armatures per side, split across a four-way crossover. As a result, you get to enjoy a wide, open soundstage with clear, airy treble and loads of detail, while the swirling, abalone-style resin faceplates mean that no two pairs look quite the same.

I'm a big fan of the Tea Pro, which I called "engagingly musical and beautifully built" in my review. Its dual 8mm dynamic drivers and six balanced armatures deliver a full, natural and lush sound, with a sub-bass presence that's always there without ever swamping the midrange. It's not the most analytical, but perfect to relax into for hours at a time.

Sources indicate that on a tighter budget? The EW300 packs a lot of tech for the cash, combining three driver types in one compact CNC-machined shell: a 10mm dynamic driver for the bass and mids, plus a 6mm planar and a piezoelectric driver working together on the highs. Swappable nozzles let you tweak the tuning, and overall, the sound from this IEM is warm, punchy and forgiving.

Out of all of ZiiGaat's recent releases, the Horizon is my favourite, earning 8 out of 10 in my review. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with two Knowles balanced armatures and two planar drivers, producing a bright-leaning, detailed sound with an impressively spacious soundstage. If you can handle a lively treble, it's an absolute treat.

According to recent reports, released in 2022, the original Cadenza is a bit of a legend, and it's still the perfect budget entry point into the world of IEMs. A single 10mm beryllium diaphragm dynamic driver, sat inside a 3D-printed resin shell, delivers a balanced sound with rich mids and clear treble, for a low, low price. Light, comfortable and a big step up from basic buds.

According to recent reports, released early this year, the Cadenza II builds on its predecessor with a upcoming 10mm titanium-coated dynamic driver and Kiwi Ears' updated KARS 2.0 bass-tuning system. My review focused on its near-neutral sound and excellent build quality, which includes a CNC-machined aluminium faceplate. If you like your sound bass-heavy, look elsewhere, but if you seek an affordable all-rounder, you're golden.

Billed as the world's first MEMS + 1DD + 3BA tribrid IEM, the Halcyon pairs a MEMS driver, a type of tech also used in hearing aids, with a 10mm dynamic driver and three balanced armatures. When testing it for my review I loved its deep, rumbly sub-bass and well-judged treble; if your playlists lean bass-heavy, it really shines.

The Odyssey pairs a custom 10mm dynamic driver with three genuine Knowles balanced armatures: two full-range drivers for the mids and an ultra-high frequency tweeter. What makes it stand out is its bass: low notes hit like a subwoofer but stop swiftly rather than lingering. That keeps the neutral midrange clean and uncluttered, with vocals that sound natural rather than plasticky.

It has been revealed that this IEM is a collab between audio brand ZiiGaat and YouTube reviewer Zeos of Z Reviews. Its single 10mm diamond-like carbon (DLC) dynamic driver serves up a hefty 16dB bass shelf, with warm, rich mids and enough treble extension to stop things getting muddy. If you like your music to rumble, this is the one.

Sources indicate that the Lush is ZiiGaat's take on a studio monitor and is designed for sound engineers and stage musicians. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with four balanced armatures via a three-way crossover, with the bass cut off at 200Hz so it doesn't bleed into the mids. Expect a neutral, coherent and versatile sound in a light, comfortable resin shell.

Sources indicate that as the name suggests, Punch Audio is all about big, bold bass, and the Patada gives that tradition a refined twist. Combining a 10mm ceramic diaphragm dynamic driver with a MEMS driver for the top end makes for a smoother, more open treble than you might expect, alongside the usual low-end thump. This is still a basshead set, then, just a slightly more well-behaved one.

The KE4 uses two 10mm dynamic drivers in an isobaric subwoofer arrangement, paired with two balanced armatures through a three-way crossover. It was an early affordable take on the 'New Meta' tuning, and when I reviewed it, I found the bass hefty but the midrange the real star: rich, layered and never boxy or thin. It's comfortable and non-fatiguing to wear, too.

CrinEar's first production IEM, the Daybreak, arrived in 2025 and is built more for enjoyment than analysis. Its combines a dynamic driver, two balanced armatures and two micro-planar drivers in a 3D-printed resin shell with aluminium faceplates. If the Reference prioritises strict accuracy, the Daybreak goes for a more engaging, crowd-pleasing sound that works with pretty much any genre.

Sources indicate that it's been a remarkable year for in-ear monitors, and Chinese brands, often lumped together under the "ChiFi "label, are a substantial reason why. Companies such as ZiiGaat, Kiwi Ears and Simgot are releasing newly introduced models at a dizzying pace, and they're no longer just competing on price.

We're seeing genuine innovation, from MEMS drivers to micro-planars, alongside a wave of collaborations with influential reviewers such as Z Reviews and HBB.

The upshot? Sound quality that would have cost a small fortune a decade ago is now available for less than a decent pair of trainers, and the gap with the big established brands keeps on shrinking.

Lucy McRae creates replicant birth bags for Blade Runner 2099 show where "violence and femininity coexist"

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles-based artist Lucy McRae has created tactile, custom-made designs for sci-fi mini-series Blade Runner 2099 that veer away from the traditionally cold and metallic aesthetic of the films.

The show, which premiered on Wednesday on Amazon Prime, is the latest in the Blade Runner universe and follows Cora, a human fugitive played by actor Hunter Schafer.

She goes undercover as a replicant – a synthetic human – blade runner with veteran replicant Olwen, played by actor Michelle Yeoh, to track down a runaway carrying a secret that could destabilise the city.

McRae joined the production in 2022 as the official futurist of the show, after showrunner Silka Luisa saw her previous work exploring the relationship between emerging technology and human biology.

Her speculative work on body futurism later became direct visual references for the show and McRae was asked to speculate on human consciousness in 50 years’ time, with a specific focus on memory, bio-engineering, replicants’ sensuality, sex and family.

“I created a world-build of those questions, through scale models, building concepts through physical materials,” McRae told Dezeen. “These ideas begin to transpire within the show.”.

McRae designed the film’s birth bags, which are incubator-like sacks used to birth or transform replicants.

She also made the crèche set, the facility and replicant birth system that support the birth bags, as well as a skin polymer traction machine that was used for healing the protagonist Cora.

McRae also designed the material and colour palette for replicants, which includes pipes, quilting and industrial materials that fit the interiors of Olwen’s spacecraft and the padding around the traction machine.

The birth bag is a newly introduced iteration of McRae’s Compression Cradle, a project presented at the 2019 Milan Triennale exhibition Broken Nature.

It was a machine that offered a simulated hug to a person craving intimacy using an inflatable device.

In Blade Runner 2099, the design scale expanded dramatically, with nine vertical Compression Cradles created inside the Tyrell building where they functioned as birth bags in the show.

Sources indicate that mcRae often describes herself as a “body architect”. At Future Sensitive, the art-research lab she leads, her work revolves around using the body as a means to speculate on the future.

A few of her recent projects have explored what McRae calls the touch crisis – the idea that, with the rise of technology, digital devices might start to vie for human affection, and physical contact with other humans might suffer as a result.

Her Heavy Duty Love, for example, created for the Venice Architecture Biennale 2021, imagines a machine replacement of a parent’s embrace in a world where humans are grown in artificial wombs.

With The Future Day Spa, meanwhile, she presented a machine that could replace human contact altogether.

McRae’s states her focus on material tactility – such as creases, wrinkles, and squishy textures – adds a femininity to the show.

The series is built on the sci-fi intellectual property that followed from the original 1982 film and its aesthetic was historically labelled as metallic, cold, slick and masculine.

It has been revealed that “The physicalisation of the work I do, the texture, achieves the femininity the show was after,” said McRae. “It’s an absolute masterpiece where both violence and femininity coexist.”.

She also believes that by domesticating science and rendering technology malleable and wet, it creates a positive future that feels within human grasp and participation.

It has been revealed that “It feels positive because it feels within my grasp. I feel I can participate and I can contribute,” stated McRae. “Whereas if it’s a future that doesn’t look or feel or belong to something that I understand, then it feels like it’s a closed door.”.

The designer stated her work for the series, and in general, aims to focus on plausible futures rather than pure fantasy, while raising open-ended questions and encouraging audiences to navigate uncertainty with hope.

“What’s important for Silka and for my work is that anything I’m dealing with is never fantasy,” noted McRae.

“I think physicalising possibility allows us to wear it, touch it and be able to get close to something that is far away but then allows us to see if it’s a fit, see if it belongs.”.

“What I’m trying to do is create opportunities for people to ask these questions themselves and for me to not answer them. It’s going to be open-ended and unanswered because we don’t live in a world where one answer or many answers fit.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quick read: Stranger Than Heaven, out 15 January 2027, trades modern Japan for five decades of period crime drama with a multilingual script and a fresh visual style, and it could be RGG Studio's biggest global hit yet.

When it comes to capturing contemporary Japan, no studio does it better than RGG Studio and its long-running Yakuza / Like A Dragon series, to the point that players are drawn in not only by its crime-based, melodramatic narrative and surreal side quests, but also by the chance to engage in virtual tourism. But its upcoming title, Stranger Than Heaven, marks a departure with a more ambitious vision, taking the player on an epic journey across five decades of early 20th-century Japan.

Industry observers note that having had the opportunity to play the game from the start at a recent hands-on event, I can say Stranger Than Heaven's story doesn't begin in Japan but in the US. While RGG Studio has specialised in making games for a Japanese audience, the past decade has seen Sega make concerted efforts to bring the Yakuza series to a global audience, with 2024's Like A Dragon: Infinite Wealth even largely taking place in Hawaii. Stranger Than Heaven also explores Japan during a period of modernisation and Western influence, as shown through its protagonist, Makoto Daito, an orphan with mixed heritage from America and Japan.

I begin with him fleeing poverty, racial discrimination and cops trying to pin a crime on him, as he stows away on a ship in San Francisco that's bound for Japan, hoping to start a new life - almost like a reverse of the immigrant American Dream narrative.

Sources indicate that in Makoto, we have a young man whose mixed heritage is made clear by his distinct blue eyes, while English is his first language, a radical change from Yakuza's typically middle-aged Japanese characters, which perhaps also reflects the game being developed by a young team, with game director Mikinobu Abe still in his twenties. Not that this was a factor in choosing a younger protagonist, since we'll also follow Makoto as he ages over five decades.

While RGG Studio's characters have always been societal outcasts as part of the criminal underworld, Makoto and another stowaway, Yu Shinjo, have their mixed heritage also single them out in Japan, as passersby don't hesitate to address them as "keto", an ethnic slur against foreigners that literally translates to "hairy barbarian". It's perhaps how he finds a kind of solidarity with the Black smugglers they have stowed away with, whose charismatic leader, Orpheus, is played by none other than Snoop Dogg.

It has been revealed that it's a casting choice that reflects Stranger Than Heaven's ambitions to appeal to a global audience, as is the game's theme song with English and Japanese lyrics performed by pop artists Tori Kelly and Ado respectively, who also have roles in the game. What that also means is that rather than having separate language dubs, the game features a single multilingual audio track, putting to bed any 'subs-versus-dubs' debates, while also arriving at a time when multilingual entertainment is getting more mainstream attention, such as the Emmy-winning Shogun.

"This decision was made to authentically portray Makoto’s dual heritage," Abe clarifies. "The narrative centres on the conflicts and challenges that arise from his identity and cultural background." That's something I was also able to appreciate in the game's opening hours set in Kokura, Fukuoka, in 1915, when Makoto is fresh off the boat and, even as someone who doesn't speak the language, I can hear how he is less confident and fluent in Japanese.

Industry observers note that "As the story moves through different eras, Makoto and Yu do not simply grow older; they gradually adapt to life in Japan," Abe explains. "We wanted to express that growth through subtle changes in their body language, mannerisms, and Japanese pronunciation. This meant carefully considering how comfortable they should appear in each scene, so that their adjustment to the environment would feel gradual and natural rather than sudden.".

During my hands-on, I also got to explore a couple of other eras, including Kure, Hiroshima in 1929 and Minami, Osaka in 1943. Notably, the passage of time is not presented in one location but in a latest city each time. While that does follow a geographical trajectory, starting from the South of Japan and working your way across the country until the story culminates in Tokyo in 1965, the cities picked also serve a narrative purpose.

In a recent development, "Kokura was a major industrial city back then, so it felt natural as the destination for someone who had stowed away on a ship," Abe explains. "We chose Kure in 1929 because it is strongly associated in Japan with yakuza stories, most famously through the film Battles Without Honor and Humanity. It has a particular significance for Makoto, who is conflicted over whether he sees himself as Japanese or American, and entering the world of the yakuza - a distinctly Japanese organisation - intensifies that struggle. At the same time, Kure was a major military port with a significant international population, giving Makoto opportunities to encounter people and experiences that reflect another side of his identity.".

With five cities, or rather districts within those cities, it also means a focus on smaller but more densely designed maps closer to Yakuza's Kamurocho compared to the larger, sprawling spaces in the more recent Like A Dragon games.

"Each upcoming city will feel genuinely distinct - not only visually, but also in the way it plays and invites exploration," Abe explains. "Kokura is a dense city where most buildings can be entered, offering players a great deal of depth to explore. Kure is a city built along a coastal mountainside, creating a vertical landscape that encourages exploration across multiple elevations. In Minami, the buildings become taller, and players can enter large multi-tenant complexes.".

It has been revealed that while there is a challenge in depicting the main cast physically ageing across five decades, it's also expressed through fashion, which really stood out as I played through three of Stranger Than Heaven's eras, with Makoto sporting a different hairstyle and clothes in each one. I also received an answer from art director Daishi Kanaya on these fashion choices, and why, unlike recent Yakuza games, the player won't have free rein to customise them.

"Rather than simply incorporating the fashions of the time, we wanted Makoto’s appearance and clothing to convey his position and situation in life, the relationships around him, and the environment he is living in at that point in the story - for example, what kind of organisation he belongs to and how much financial security he has," Kanaya explains. "We have not made his appearance customisable by the player. We felt it was notable for us to present the version of Makoto that is most appropriate to each stage of his life, so that players can more strongly experience his journey as a person.".

Stranger Than Heaven's ambitions are also evident in the technical advances made with RGG Studio's decade-old in-house Dragon Engine. While recent games have been made as cross-platform releases, this one is coming exclusively to current-gen, which has allowed the studio to incorporate more complex human behaviour to make the world feel more alive, and to use advanced post-processing and lighting to elevate the visuals. This is especially great during the game's lengthy cutscenes, something the studio already prides itself on doing, which also show its flair and understanding of drama, as these aren't just reserved for bombastic action sequences but really shine during quiet human moments, such as Makoto's first meeting with Tae, played exquisitely by Shogun's Moeka Hoshi.

According to recent reports, however, Abe clarifies that he also worked closely with Kanaya to develop a distinct visual style that wasn't just about high-fidelity photorealism. "Kanaya has a background in oil painting, while I come from a filmmaking background, so we brought our respective perspectives together as we searched for a visual identity unique to this title," he explains. "We studied vintage lenses, old films, record covers, and paintings from the period, trying to understand what made those works feel so distinctive - the way they captured light, the softness of their focus, and the texture they created.".

Recent findings suggest that as a upcoming game that sets itself apart from the Yakuza series, even if it's still technically in the same universe, portraying what will be the origins of the Tojo Clan, Stranger Than Heaven has been built from the ground up, a change from the studio's approach to efficiently recycling assets for its successive Yakuza titles. That includes a radically different, if at times awkward, dual-limbed combat system that I previously grappled with at Gamescom, as well as many more new bespoke animations, including everyday actions like Makoto eating food from a stall or drinking from a fountain.

Recent findings suggest that "While some motions from previous titles were used as a starting point, they were extensively revised - often to the point that their origins would be unrecognisable. This was necessary because Makoto, his world, and the story surrounding him represent a major departure from our previous games. The way people walk and carry themselves differs from a modern setting, and Makoto’s behaviour and reactions to his environment are specific to his character and era. As a result, we needed to create and adjust the animations accordingly.".

In the case of the combat system, while I still found it a bit of a struggle, especially against multiple foes, it's also intentional so that you're not just easily smacking down enemies like Yakuza's Kazuma Kiryu with simple but powerful inputs. "We took a lot of inspiration from Japanese yakuza films and found how raw their action can feel," Abe explains. "The characters are not martial arts masters; their fights are often desperate and unrefined. They grab each other’s clothes, struggle at close range, and use whatever is around them. It is not simply a matter of throwing punches and kicks. In these films, violence often carries a real sense of life-or-death tension - it is a matter of killing or being killed. Creating that tension, and allowing players to experience Makoto’s fear, desperation, and gradual growth firsthand, was at the core of our approach to the tone of the combat.".

Recent findings suggest that while a lot of research was carried out to ensure environments were authentic to their time period, the game also carries the disclaimer that it is "in no way a reproduction of actual history", which perhaps also gives it licence to be a little anachronistic, such as having Snoop Dogg rapping a few bars in the title song, which musically also has some hip-hop influences, despite the genre originating in the US in the 1970s outside of Stranger Than Heaven's setting. Snoop himself might also be a bit of a distraction - as has been the controversial casting of the late Tupac Shakur, who wasn't shown during this hands-on - as there's a scene where Orpheus teaches Makoto how to roll his own tobacco (indicative of its time period; smoking in this game actually gives you buffs), though given one of the ingredients is "grass", I couldn't help but be taken out of the moment and think, yep, that's Snoop.

"What mattered to us was depicting a reimagined world and era with a sense of realism to depict what we wanted as a gameplay experience and narrative," Abe explains. "The same approach applied to the casting of Snoop Dogg. Orpheus would teach Makoto how to survive in Japan and how to make money through music and show business, and at the same time, he is a smuggler who brings Makoto from America to Japan. He needed to be someone formidable - someone with musical talent who could also handle emotionally demanding scenes. So from early on, we had the idea that it would be amazing if Snoop Dogg could play the role.".

That still leaves the question of setting a story across a period of Japanese history that, while full of cultural change, is also controversial. Considering that Stranger Than Heaven's story depicts racial discrimination in Japan, I can't help but think of the multigenerational drama Pachinko, also beginning in 1915, depicting the treatment of Korean immigrants in Japan during its imperial rule of Korea, which seems entirely absent. You could also argue that the story intentionally skims over more controversial moments in the country's history, notably omitting the 1930s, when it invaded China, and ending before the civil unrest of the late 1960s.

Ultimately, Abe argues that the focus is more on Makoto's personal journey than on recounting history. "The game does touch on historical events, for example, its 1943 Osaka setting takes place during wartime, but the narrative is fundamentally centred on Makoto Daito’s life rather than depicting history in detail," he explains. "Even during war, which profoundly affects the lives of everyone, people still live their own individual lives, and Makoto is no different.".

Stranger Than Heaven is then as ambitious as it is contentious, but through its Japanese-Western cultural exchanges and a significant upgrade of visuals and systems, it has the potential to be RGG Studio's biggest global hit to date.

Stranger Than Heaven releases on 15 January 2027 for Xbox Series X/S, PS5, and PC.

"How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.
  • According to recent reports, the last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in New York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught.
  • During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.

According to recent reports, the last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in New York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught. How had these young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?

During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.

Sources indicate that having assumed these conversations had become an expected part of design education, I was taken aback by how little the students cared. Instead, they were far more concerned with securing and keeping jobs in an increasingly precarious industry.

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience.

According to recent reports, “How do you expect us to make any difference if this is how the industry works?” one asked. Another just wanted to know how to earn a living, without upsetting their employers.

These were excellent questions, particularly as designers now compete with artificial intelligence capable of executing instructions at extraordinary speed. If design is reduced to following briefs and producing outputs, what space is there for a designer to effect any structural change?

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience. Designers are trained to solve problems, yet rarely encouraged to question who defined them, whose interests they serve, or whether they should exist at all. They are commissioned to make products more sustainable without questioning production volumes, or improve services without examining the policies that make them inaccessible.

In a recent development, I often say design is a series of well-informed decisions. Every object, building and service emerges from decisions about resources, labor, budgets and the conditions of life.

It has been revealed that designers participate in these decisions, although they rarely control all of them. So where does their power begin and end?

In a recent development, imagine a design studio commissioned by a city to address extreme heat in a low-income neighborhood. The brief requests solar-powered cooling shelters and shaded public spaces, with a fixed budget and deadline.

It has been revealed that during research, the designers discover that the proposed shelters would be too far from elderly residents most vulnerable to heat, while existing community centers could accommodate cooling facilities at a lower cost. What should they do? Follow the brief, collect their fees and pretend their hands are tied? Refuse the commission, leaving another studio to complete the work, perhaps feeling rebellious for a moment?

There is a third possibility. They could show the city why its proposal would fail to reach its intended beneficiaries and present an alternative within the same budget. Working with residents and community organizations, they could identify accessible locations, compare costs and demonstrate how the alternative better meets the city’s objectives.

The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Here we see a tangible expansion of design as a civic responsibility. Designers can use their expertise to bring communities into decisions that affect their lives, improving outcomes while sharing decision-making power.

And if the city insists on its original proposal? The client controls the budget. A junior designer acting alone may have little negotiating power.

According to recent reports, but a studio can incorporate community research into its contracts before work begins, negotiate a paid investigation phase and require the client to review evidence and alternatives before approving the design. Of course, this doesn’t guarantee agreement, but it makes critical inquiry a recognised part of the commission.

In a recent development, design is a practice of applied imagination: understanding interconnected systems to intentionally shape the conditions of life. In this example, designers would examine the relationships between urban planning, public health, housing, energy and community governance. Their value lies partly in identifying what the original commission overlooked and developing viable possibilities with the people affected.

Thanks to the work of people like Victor Papanek, Tony Fry, Ezio Manzini and Arturo Escobar, by now it’s well understood that design has the capacity to shape the world but remains complicit in ecological and social destruction. The challenge today is to translate that knowledge into professional authority, economic leverage and meaningful participation in the decisions that will determine our collective futures.

Likewise, advocates of participatory design have long argued for involving people affected by design decisions. The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Meeting these challenges requires rethinking design education. Designers need to learn to investigate the historical conditions behind a problem, understand ecological and economic relationships, and work alongside communities to develop alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that design can shape community-owned infrastructure, food systems and forms of local governance as well as products and buildings. These are tangible fields of work requiring collaboration and shared authority.

We should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Of course, clients may refuse evidence, and insecure workers cannot always risk confrontation. Already there is too much pressure on Gen Z to save the world; we should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Sources indicate that studios, educators and commissioners must create paid roles and decision-making processes that give designers genuine influence. What if, for example, investigating the risks and assumptions behind a brief became an essential professional service, one that designers were commissioned and compensated to provide?

I keep thinking about those students at SVA, afraid of being considered difficult. We have taught them how to execute decisions without adequately preparing them to participate in making them. If designers are to take responsibility for their role in shaping the systems that govern our lives, they need a say in the decisions that produce those systems.

Industry observers note that in the near future, success would mean residents gaining influence over where public money goes, with designers helping turn their priorities into lasting changes in public planning. This is design as a civic responsibility, and a meaningful distinction from machines optimized to execute instructions. To design possible futures, we must grow the agency designers hold, and the collective power they can help communities to build.

Céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian designer, artist, writer, educator and speaker based in Newly introduced York City, whose work focuses on climate complications and social justice. She is the founder of Slow Factory, a non-profit education and research platform that teaches about regenerative design. Her writing has appeared in The Cut, Vogue, Elle, Refinery29 and New York Magazine, among others. Her first book, A Woman Is a School, was published in 2024, and her upcoming book, Designing Possible Futures, is due for publication in 2027.

Side stitch, stomach cramp, side ache — whatever you wanna call it, that mid-run pain in your tum can seriously *cramp* your runner’s high.

This pesky prob that plagues runners and athletes all over has a scientific name: Exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP). Though experts don’t know exactly what causes it, they have some ideas and tips about how to stop it.

Before you double-over during your next marathon, here’s what to know.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod says tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

According to recent reports, this common prob has been around for ages — the first historical mention is from ancient Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder. Yet, scientists still haven’t reached a consensus on its exact cause. We know that it affects up to 70% of runners each year.

It’s also more likely to occur on the right side.

A stiff spine or poor posture (according to older research from 2010) could contribute to side stitches – but TBH, the pros don’t know for sure.

In a recent development, according to a 2022 review, researchers also think a side stitch might be caused by your right foot hitting the ground while you breathe out, irritating a phrenic nerve. Researchers think this, in turn, may bother the lining of your abdomen (particularly on the lower right side). Since most people are right-foot dominant, this is one possible explanation.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a big race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

Industry observers note that consider working on your running form or breathing to reduce the risk of experiencing a side stitch. Staying hydrated and avoiding huge meals pre-run may also help. Consider working with a physical therapist or personal trainer if your complications persist.

If you experience pain under your breastbone when running, visit a doctor asap.

#149877. After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • It has been revealed that at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

It has been revealed that at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Recent findings suggest that conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

As the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

In a recent development, black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

According to recent reports, that is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

Industry observers note that the data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research indicates that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

Industry observers note that that matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

It has been revealed that the lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Sources indicate that faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

According to recent reports, black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

According to recent reports, it’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he intends to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.

Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.

However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.

What Ratti has revealed so far is that he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach to the event.

Specifically, he will use an AI assistant, aiming to challenge traditional approaches to developing exhibitions by highlighting emerging tools that can help curators.

“I am delighted to take on the direction of the Seoul Biennale and to explore the future of cities together with the Seoul Metropolitan Government,” states Carlo Ratti.

“Seoul is perhaps the best place in the world to ask how artificial intelligence and the collective wisdom of its citizens might shape the city together,” he continued.

“At the upcoming pre-biennale event, we will begin to introduce the people who will join us, and I think there will be a few surprises – one assistant curator isn’t even human!”.

Ratti is an Italian architect and engineer, and director of his eponymous studio Carlo Ratti Associati. He is also a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

He was appointed by Seoul mayor Oh Se Hoon, succeeding British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who curated the 2025 event.

Heatherwick centred the event on a long, four-storey-high wall displaying images that reflected the ideals of his Humanise campaign.

The Seoul Biennale was established in 2017 by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as a festival of international architecture and urbanism.

“The Seoul Biennale is a place where architects and citizens from around the world think together about the future of cities and explore new possibilities,” remarked mayor Oh.

“Together with general director Carlo Ratti, who has connected architecture, cities, and technology, we will prepare so that the sixth Seoul Biennale offers a new perspective on cities and architecture and a meaningful experience for citizens.”.

Ratti’s previous curatorial experience includes the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025, for which the theme was Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. It explored how architecture can be adapted to increasingly unstable living environments through cross-disciplinary collaboration.

At the time, Ratti said, “Dezeen killed the traditional form of the biennale“.

The architect’s other recent projects include the French Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka and a proposal for a children’s hospital housed in a one-kilometre “green ring”.

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

We checked in with a doctor to find out.

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” claims Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”.

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:.

Vukasinov says that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:.

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

It has been revealed that remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a significant hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

#149874. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

According to recent reports, “The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

It has been revealed that although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sources indicate that sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin indicates.

In a recent development, because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin notes. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

In a recent development, women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, says Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin says. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin says. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

Sources indicate that that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health problems.

According to recent reports, if left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, claims Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra states, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Industry observers note that because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar claims. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research highlights that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s key to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sources indicate that A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that right now average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

According to recent reports, deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Recent findings suggest that right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Sources indicate that points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

In a recent development, timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:.

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

Sources indicate that this is the most notable financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Recent findings suggest that websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Customers Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:.

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sources indicate that sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Sources indicate that contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Recent findings suggest that timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:.

Industry observers note that here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In a recent development, in very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

It has been revealed that A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

In a recent development, the slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

In a recent development, “Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” indicates Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo states it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

According to recent reports, while its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”.

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily swiftly after washing,” Macedo states, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”.

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:.

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she claims can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

Industry observers note that “If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”.

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets claims that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.
