📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The gold standard business class redemption using British Airways Avios.

Business Class Product Worldwide.

In a recent development, picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Recent findings suggest that qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

Sources indicate that the critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Recent findings suggest that citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

It has been revealed that capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy® Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

Sources indicate that this is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

It has been revealed that british Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

Award Price: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person, one-way. Taxes and fees on Qatar-operated awards are minimal — typically under $100 — because Qatar charges no fuel surcharges. A couple flies QSuites for 150,000 Avios plus roughly $150 in taxes total.

The CPP: At the midpoint cash value of $6,500, you're getting 8.7 cents per Avios — nearly nine times what most people assume a loyalty point is worth. At $10,000, you're at 13.3 cents per point. Even at the conservative end, 6.7 cents per point makes this one of the top redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem.

What the Experience Actually Looks Like:.

Recent findings suggest that you arrive at JFK and access Qatar's partner lounge before departure — a preview of what's to come. Once aboard, you're shown to a fully enclosed private suite with a sliding door, direct aisle access from every seat, a large personal screen, and a seat that converts to a lie-flat bed stretching over 6 feet. The bedding is genuine Westin Heavenly quality. You and your travel companion request the Double Bed configuration — the center divider lowers, and you're sharing a full-width sleeping surface mid-flight.

According to recent reports, dining is a la carte, on-demand — no set meal times. The wine list is legitimate. The service is attentive without being intrusive.

If you've added a Doha stopover to your ticket, you deplane into Al Mourjan Business Lounge — a cavernous, beautifully designed space with dedicated dining, shower suites, and quiet zones. It is, consistently, one of the top-rated airport lounges on earth.

Sources indicate that this is the experience your 75,000 points buy. No amount of economy class upgrades gets you here.

Avoid this: Using Marriott Bonvoy® as your primary transfer path. The 3:1 ratio means you need 225,000 Bonvoy points to get 75,000 Avios. Marriott points are valuable for hotel redemptions — burning them at a 3:1 ratio for airline miles is rarely optimal unless you have a massive surplus.

Avoid this: Waiting for a sale or hoping for better availability. Qatar doesn't run award sales. The award chart is fixed, and availability only decreases over time on popular routes. The readers who say "I'll book when something comes up" are the ones sharing their story about the year they almost flew QSuites.

Remember: Miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your Privilege Club account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every 36 months. A single small transaction resets the clock.

Sources indicate that this redemption earns a **Moderate** difficulty rating, and that's honest. Not all Qatar 777s have QSuites. Check SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to confirm the specific aircraft configuration. Routes to major US gateways (JFK, IAD, ORD, IAH, LAX, DFW) typically operate QSuites-equipped aircraft.

#149835. Latest Update: It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

📅 21 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2297 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

📅 21 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day.
  • I have just seen Michael (the fresh Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release.
  • According to recent reports, on screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

I have just seen Michael (the fresh Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

According to recent reports, on screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She states almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

“There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she states. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s important to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”.

According to recent reports, long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

“My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she says. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”.

Long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

According to recent reports, “The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I noted money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”.

Industry observers note that once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”.

Now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft upcoming stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

In a recent development, “This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”.

Sources indicate that in talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

Sources indicate that she laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

In 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

Recent findings suggest that “The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”.

Industry observers note that that clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

Industry observers note that “I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is big. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She claims all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

In the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she states. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”.

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

Long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

“I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”.

In a recent development, the memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

“In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she states. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother mentioned it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”.

It has been revealed that that an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a new idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

But Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole upcoming body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she says. “I find the balance.”.

Beauty was never her primary currency, she says. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

“Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she indicates. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the significant stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”.

Architecture, Cooperation, and the Public Realm.

It has been revealed that the relationship between architecture and collective life emerged through several announcements this week. The Lisbon Architecture Triennale selected CO-OP as the theme for its 2028 edition, with Chief Curator Joaquim Moreno proposing cooperation as a framework for examining housing, production, ownership, governance, and shared forms of living. The curatorial programme will explore how collective action shapes the production and use of space, extending the discussion from domestic arrangements to labour, landscape, and the common good. In Mexico, COLECTIVO C733 was named the inaugural recipient of the Siza Award for Public Architecture, established by the Serralves Foundation to recognize architectural generosity and engagement with public space. The practice's portfolio, which includes markets, cultural facilities, transport infrastructure, and public landscapes across Mexico, reflects the award's interest in architecture's relationship with local communities and their environments.

Building and Urban Systems in Transition.

In a recent development, at COP31 in Antalya, the built environment featured in discussions on climate action through initiatives addressing energy efficiency, electrification, and urban resilience. The Turkish Presidency introduced the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, a voluntary framework targeting a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock by 2035, compared with 2020 levels. Developed in collaboration with UNEP's Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction, the initiative outlines strategies for building renovation, reduced energy demand, efficient electrification, and improved building performance. Discussions also addressed how national climate commitments can translate into local investments in housing, infrastructure, and adaptation, while the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF) was presented as a mechanism to connect cities with existing financing and technical support. Despite these sector-specific initiatives, disagreements over fossil fuels and climate finance prevented agreement on the proposed Antalya Pact, leaving broader questions about the international energy transition unresolved.

Industry observers note that questions of environmental performance and resource use also appeared among the projects recognized at the 2026 World Architecture Festival. The World Building of the Year award went to The Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects in Indore, India, whose stepped configuration draws on the spatial tradition of Indian stepwells while integrating courtyards that bring natural light into its interior spaces. The World Interior of the Year, &Matcha Three Yards by MLA at Home in the Philippines, uses open spaces, vegetation, water, and changing natural conditions to shape a small tea shop as a shared neighbourhood environment. Other winning projects approached environmental systems through different scales and disciplines, including Terreform ONE's Coding Kelp: Artificial Reef and Data Archive, named Future Project of the Year, and Natureza Urbana's Doca Linear Park in Brazil, awarded Landscape of the Year.

Qatar Museums Unveils Gerhard Richter's Permanent Doha Pavilion, Designed in Collaboration with Selldorf Architects.

Qatar Museums has unveiled Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter, a permanent, site-specific structure conceived by the German artist in collaboration with Selldorf Architects. Located in MIA Park, outside the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha, the pavilion brings together a collection of Richter's paintings and sculptures, including a latest work developed specifically for the space. Its hexagonal structure translates the artist's investigations into abstraction and perception into an architectural form, with six exterior walls featuring geometric patterns derived from his Patterns series. The design draws connections between Richter's mathematical approach to image-making and the repeating geometries of Islamic art. Realized as a legacy initiative of the Qatar-Germany 2017 Year of Culture, the pavilion joins other permanent public artworks in MIA Park and was unveiled as part of Qatar Creates Fall/Winter 2026–27, coinciding with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar.

Memphis Art Museum Opens Fresh Herzog & de Meuron-Designed Building on the Mississippi River.

It has been revealed that the Memphis Art Museum will open its new building on the banks of the Mississippi River on December 6, 2026. Designed by Herzog & de Meuron, with archimania as architect of record, the project expands the museum's gallery space by 50 percent and increases its free public areas sixfold. Constructed primarily from laminated mass timber, the new building forms a two-acre urban campus with a 50,000-square-foot rooftop art park, a riverfront amphitheater, and a 10,000-square-foot community courtyard. Its inaugural program includes Making Beauty: Hooks Brothers Studio, 1907–1984, an exhibition of more than 150 photographs documenting Black life and culture in the urban South, alongside 15 presentations from the museum's collection and four site-specific commissions.

Tulsa's Gilcrease Museum to Reopen in March 2027 Following Six-Year Closure.

After six years of closure, the Gilcrease Museum in Tulsa, Oklahoma, is set to reopen in March 2027 with a upcoming purpose-built building. Designed by SmithGroup in consultation with the Osage Nation, the museum will house a collection of more than 300,000 objects spanning 12,000 years of art, history, and culture across the Americas. The collection includes Indigenous art and cultural materials, colonial Latin American works, American portraiture, and art of the American West. Located on a 460-acre campus overlooking the Osage Hills, the museum will also connect its galleries with the surrounding landscape through 14 miles of hiking and biking trails. Founded in 1949 by Thomas Gilcrease, a citizen of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, the institution's reopening marks a new phase for its collection and research activities.

#149831. How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1480 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting.
  • Recent findings suggest that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships.
  • Recent findings suggest that going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

Recent findings suggest that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to important resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a substantial role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

Recent findings suggest that going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

The reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

That can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman claims. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

Ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

In a recent development, going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

Moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

Industry observers note that again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

In a recent development, maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

You could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

If you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your plans could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

In a recent development, that said, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, says Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

It has been revealed that feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, states Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

According to recent reports, still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

Goodman says the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

Yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, claims Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

Sources indicate that all of that is normal, says Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

Sources indicate that you can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact strategy you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

Sources indicate that if this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, notes Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

According to recent reports, remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

Magnus Ditlev Sets New Iron-Distance World Best With 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida.
  • One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back.
  • Florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN).

One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

Florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

However, ahead of Kona, Ditlev said he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

According to recent reports, ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

Industry observers note that by the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

What Goes into Visualizing a Upcoming City?

Planning an entirely newly introduced city means considering several elements together:.

Planning an entirely new city means considering several elements together:.

Buildings and public spaces: How buildings relate to streets, squares, parks and surrounding neighborhoods; Movement and infrastructure: How roads, pedestrian routes and public transport connect different parts of the development; Landscape and surroundings: How green spaces, existing terrain and the wider environment fit into the strategy; Changes over time: How visual material can be updated as building designs, infrastructure and other parts of the masterplan evolve.

Recent findings suggest that getting these relationships right helps people understand how a proposed development is intended to function as a place. It also means keeping visualizations aligned with the latest plans, without presenting undecided parts of the project as finished designs.

Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.
  • Recent findings suggest that after our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew.
  • In a recent development, it felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.

Recent findings suggest that after our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew. I wasn’t so sure. For months, it had felt like my husband Ethan and I were two bodies fumbling to find each other in the dark. At home, our orbits rarely intersected. My eyes barely landed on Ethan. Once, he didn’t realize I was right behind him and he closed the door on me.

In a recent development, it felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble. We weathered life-altering challenges together in our 20s and 30s due to my whole-body symptoms from endometriosis, adenomyosis, early menopause, and a medical system that trivialized them all. My condition rattled our intimacy, upended my career, and made Ethan my caretaker. Being undiagnosed for decades also cost us my fertility, depleting my ovarian reserve and leading to miscarriage after miscarriage with IVF and IUIs.

Though we weren’t living the life we dreamed, and I felt guilty for the weight I foisted on Ethan, we managed to maintain the joie de vivre we’d had since we first met—until we turned to surrogacy.

Industry observers note that our decision to opt for an egg donor and a surrogate was an act of compromise. Though I’d always been ambivalent about motherhood, the idea of coparenting with Ethan had gradually filled me with tenderness and curiosity. But by then, after years of illness, I wanted a hysterectomy. Ethan still really wanted to be a dad. Neither of us wanted to jeopardize my wellness with more hormonal treatments and pregnancy losses, so we took what people called the “easy way out.” Though I was criticized by my doctors for giving up on my eggs and my uterus “too soon,” our decision to pursue surrogacy felt liberating—at first.

According to recent reports, we thought finding a gestational surrogate would be the hardest part. Turns out, we were wrong. Instead, we were totally unprepared for the ways surrogacy was going to change our marriage.

Recent findings suggest that our first surrogacy experience was the kind we now caution other intended parents against. We entrusted an agency with our fate and our funds, putting them in charge of introducing us to a surrogate and acting as the intermediary who would reimburse her for pregnancy-related expenses on our behalf. At the time, we were unaware of their proven fraudulent history.

It has been revealed that not only were Ethan and I new to surrogacy, but we also felt vulnerable—maybe even desperate. We were privileged to have found someone who wanted to do this for us, and we wanted to be generous and grateful. You also don’t have much control when your baby is in someone else’s womb and your funds are in a corporation’s bank account. So we ignored the red flags we noticed with the agency’s inflated reimbursements and our surrogate’s jarring mood fluctuations.

In a recent development, if we’d shared our worries with each other early on, we may have had a chance to course-correct. At least I wouldn’t have felt so alone carrying this angst in my bones. At one of our second-trimester ultrasounds, I resented Ethan for being his jovial self while he talked to our active baby boy through the screen as I stood hunched against the wall, struggling to feel present. It wasn’t just that the pregnancy felt unbearably abstract for me as a mother who didn’t contribute her genes or her womb; I was also increasingly skeptical of the agency and walking on eggshells with our surrogate, who’d keep us at arm’s length one week and accuse us of not being supportive enough the next. I’d never gotten this far in a pregnancy and it should have been a happy time. Instead, I bottled up my distress and couldn’t breathe from the weight of it.

During our first surrogacy experience, Ethan let me bear the brunt of the conversations with our surrogate. He thought he had a supportive role, but his not being in the foreground put extra weight on my shoulders and took my time, energy, and headspace while sparing him. I was also the one who handled all the legal and financial paperwork, and the communication with the agency. Ethan was grateful and proud of me for managing what he considered more in my wheelhouse than his, but I felt paralyzing stress and resentment having to tackle these hard tasks on my own at such a vulnerable time.

Our breaking point was brought on by our different ways of grieving. While I naturally tend to dig deep into painful topics and emotions to make sense of them, Ethan prefers to compartmentalize. At the hospital after the delivery, Ethan preferred to leave the room when I stayed to spend a few minutes with our stillborn. I wanted the loss to feel more tangible, while he wanted to hold onto the joy from other memories, like when we saw him on ultrasounds. Neither of us was wrong, but we were disconnected.

Industry observers note that the months that followed were agony because none of the doctors would counsel us on why our baby had died simply because I wasn’t the pregnant patient, as though we weren’t his parents and didn’t have the right to know. I spiraled into depression and was furious every time Ethan would tell his parents that we were fine. He didn’t want to burden them, but I didn’t want to mask our reality for the sake of others’ comfort. For 24 years—through long distance, sickness, and grief—we’d been the “strong couple” who never argued. Now, in the complexity of surrogacy, we kept snapping at each other because Ethan needed a semblance of normalcy and I needed to dwell in darkness.

So how do you come back to each other when who you were didn’t survive? Over nearly a year, thanks to our self-awareness, deep respect for one another, and therapy (which Ethan hated attending but did when required), we made three tiny shifts that saved our marriage.

When we met our second surrogate through a more ethical, transparent, and supportive agency that did not demand funds in trust, Ethan and I formed a true trio with her. It helped that she considered us a team and wanted our involvement in appointments, decisions, and her daily life. She’d use the word “together” so often that it initially triggered us; it felt so foreign to us after our first surrogacy journey, and we couldn’t tell which of the two experiences was the anomaly. Ethan made it a priority to participate in our conversations and replied to our group texts if I couldn’t. We all shared freely—our fears, dreams, victories, recipes, and silly inside jokes—and the three of us built an intimacy I never expected. When it was just the two of us, our surrogate was never far from our thoughts, as if our marriage had expanded to include her.

It has been revealed that ethan also started to help me with the challenging legal and financial tasks. He kept up with emails he was CC’ed on during the day and sat with me if we had paperwork to tackle, his hand on my back if I got overwhelmed.

When we lost our baby with our second surrogate at the end of the first trimester, we grieved as a unit. Our trio sat intertwined, our hands piled on my lap. At home, Ethan was more receptive to my needs on my bad days. Just watching him witness me in those moments, even if all he did was listen and sigh, brought us closer together. I was more understanding when he clung to his social activities to blow off steam. Ethan was more honest with family and friends about our emotional and financial distress. He agreed to ask for help and for a loan to help us get back on our feet after two surrogacy journeys and thirteen years of fertility and ongoing health expenses.

Recent findings suggest that we decided not to talk about surrogacy on weekends or right before bed to give our nervous systems a chance to unwind. Dark humor helped us grieve: We’d sometimes whisper jaded comments to each other when triggered. When we imagine something creative we would have done with our kid, we say, “File it under never!” During the holidays, Ethan toasted me with, “Cheers to not losing a child this Christmas!” Holding space for our contrasting ways of grieving and meeting in the middle helped dissolve the resentment and tension between us.

Sources indicate that fertility treatments and surrogacy can become all-consuming for a couple, especially after decades of illness and loss. Being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after our first surrogacy experience further shook my identity. We started making a conscious effort to remember what was special about our life and our love before all this. We are more than what we carry and what we’ve lost.

Besides carving out periods of play, nature, and grief-free talk, we also pushed ourselves to keep money aside for leisure and travel—not just for our living expenses and surrogacy costs—so we can look forward to something in our calendar and savor fresh experiences together.

We found, though, that the least daunting way of rebuilding our future is to simply take care of our present. Often, all we can handle is the next half-hour: where to take a walk, what to make for supper, how to support each other right then. I worked hard to keep my eyes focused on Ethan until it became natural again. Even now, as we grapple with whether and how to continue with our surrogacy journey, when we start acting like passing ships because of our full heads and aching hearts, we drop everything, hug, touch.

I never expected our strong marriage to be impacted by the most tender gift we gave each other: the chance to grow our family through surrogacy. We’d naively thought what awaited us would be easier than the road that led there. Our experiences with surrogacy have changed how we show up for each other, both in joy and in grief.

Sources indicate that I can’t say for certain that our marriage is now strong enough to survive anything that lies ahead. What I know is this: We’ve built what we’ll need to recalibrate our direction to find each other in the dark.
